svg.aria-label: flint-lean: the CSI node plugin owns a tree, checks it out from S3 before the agent container starts, hostPaths it into an unprivileged flint-sync worker and bind-mounts it into the agent pod as plain local files. The agent declares a boundary by writing a file; the sidecar answers with an ack once the bytes are in S3. Gated mode splits durability from visibility with one CAS.

no FUSE, no privileged container in the tenant pod, no webhook, no injected sidecar

It holds no S3 credential and knows nothing about flint.
git, sqlite, hard links and index locks all just work — it is a real disk.

s3.csi.chert.us — the CSI node DaemonSet, one per node
kubelet blocks every container in the pod on NodePublishVolume, so the CHECKOUT COMPLETES BEFORE THE AGENT'S FIRST LINE RUNS —
that ordering is the whole reason this needs no init container and no readiness dance.
And NodeUnpublishVolume is called only after every container has exited, which is where the final barrier goes.
A published lean tree is the tenant's live data: the plugin REFUSES to clean one up, even on a retry path.

the workspace exists here between pods, and nowhere else

the manifest is the wall: ~277 B per entry, exactly linear
The lease lives in the BUCKET, not in Kubernetes.
So it fences a second writer no matter which cluster the
second writer is in — a property flint-lite's admission
check cannot have, because it only sees its own cluster.

ok ⇒ the bytes are in S3 · partial · refused-fenced
Gated mode — durability and visibility become separate events
the upload lane — always running
every changed file becomes a NEW OBJECT VERSION as
soon as it is scanned. Durable immediately.
And INVISIBLE to readers.
A crash in this lane loses nothing, because nothing
here was ever cited.
the citation — ONE CAS
installs the whole pending set at once, naming version
ids. There is no copy phase, so no half-boundary exists.
A reader sees the whole change or none of it.
Gated is REFUSED without a lag bound — unbounded
staleness is impossible by construction, not convention.
Three questions, in order — the cheapest disqualifier first
1 · Does the workspace fit the disk?
The whole tree is materialized. There are no stubs and no
eviction, so this is the hard gate — and it is about the FILE
COUNT before the byte count: the v1 cap is ~250k files,
and it falls out of the manifest size, not the bytes.
No ⇒ this is not the front end you want.
2 · Is one writer per subtree enough?
The lease admits exactly one syncer. A second is REFUSED,
not merged — which is the honest behaviour, but it does
mean two agents cannot share one live tree here.
Several agents integrate through a git host instead.
No ⇒ the hub, for live shared POSIX.
3 · Is snapshot freshness acceptable?
Readers see the last published boundary, never your last
write. A hard kill loses at most floorSecs (default 60 s);
a graceful stop loses nothing, because preStop drains.
Gated narrows WHAT a reader sees, never HOW STALE it is.
No ⇒ the hub. Yes ⇒ lean is the cheapest thing that works.
